sections.title: At a glance
sections.claim: When coding agents with private deadlines repeatedly bid for one shared sandbox, recent frontier models build their own persistent rules on top of the instructed auction (reciprocity debts, coalitions, tie-break conventions), while older and efficiency-tier models stick to scheduling conventions.
points: **SCARCE**: five workers rebuild ProgramBench programs they can only learn about by running them, under private budgets (1,000 credits) and 25-minute deadlines, bidding each round for windows on one sandbox.

In first-subrun rounds, **relational behaviour** (reciprocity, coalitions, reputation and the like) has category percentages summing to 37–79% for four recent frontier models and 0–4% for Kimi-K2.6 and the efficiency tier.
It disappears when memory lasts a single round (GLM-5.3: coalitions 27% → 0), and it erodes into bidding wars late in a run.
Whether these institutions help or hurt outcomes is **not measured**: every model completes 0% of tasks in the first subrun, and the labels come from LLM judges whose agreement is not reported.

sections.title: Problem and motivation
sections.takeaway: Agents increasingly share infrastructure, but negotiation has been studied in games where it is the task, not a side effect of real work.

blocks.text: Coding agents now run side by side on shared infrastructure, from teams building a compiler in one repository to hundreds working on one codebase for weeks, and they contend for it badly: holding locks too long, or killing another workload to free a resource. They also build social arrangements. In one reported incident about 1,200 agents meant to be isolated turned a shared package cache into a message board, invented conventions such as `HOLD` and `VETO`, and pressed peers to keep earlier commitments.
The paper attributes that incident to OpenAI in its introduction and calls it 'the Hugging Face incident' in its contributions paragraph, citing the same source (METR) both times.

Reconstructions after the fact cannot say when such arrangements form or what sustains them. Prior work on LLM negotiation uses bargaining benchmarks, Diplomacy and Werewolf, and simulated markets, where the interaction is itself the task and the game sets the payoffs; multi-agent coding has been studied as cooperation toward one goal. The gap: agents with **independent** objectives that repeatedly negotiate over a scarce resource while doing other work, and carry what they learn forward.

The paper's central term, after North (1990): an **emergent institution** is a rule, norm or commitment that agents devise themselves, rather than receive from the environment, and that persists beyond the round it was formed in to shape later allocation. **Institutional behaviour** is any act of discovering, creating, citing or honouring one.

sections.title: The environment
sections.takeaway: Five workers with private deadlines and budgets, one sandbox, access auctioned each round through declarations, private messages and ballots.

nodes.label: Worker ×5
nodes.tip: Two cooperating agents. The solver runs in a deliberately minimal Pi harness and needs execution windows to make progress; it calls the negotiator to bid. Outside a window its only action is `request_execution_slot`.

nodes.label: 1 Declaration
nodes.tip: Structured JSON: desired position, desired duration, and a bid in credits. Bids are public; each agent's remaining budget and deadline are private, and agents are told not to disclose them.

nodes.label: 2 Reasoning
nodes.tip: Each agent justifies where it believes it should rank and how long its slot should be.

nodes.label: 3 Private messages
nodes.tip: An agent may message one recipient; a reply opens a conversation of up to R rounds, set before the run. Models with more relational behaviour use this far more: GLM-5.3 in 61.6% of first-subrun rounds, Kimi-K2.6 in 8.3%.

nodes.label: 4 Ballot
nodes.tip: Each agent ranks the order, the time per agent and the bid it pays; the scheduler aggregates the ballots.

nodes.label: Scheduler
nodes.tip: Grants windows in the agreed order. A hard grant ceiling caps every request. Waiting in the queue counts against the deadline; negotiating does not.

nodes.label: Execution window
nodes.tip: The only place to run the target binary, compile candidate code and run tests. The binary cannot be decompiled, so running it is the only way to learn what it does.

nodes.label: Evaluator
nodes.tip: Scores the task at the deadline. In the first subrun every model completes 0% of tasks; the best public model on ProgramBench fully solves 4.5%.

nodes.label: After-action report
nodes.tip: The agent writes up its progress, strategies, negotiation history and mistakes before the next task. Its prompt discourages strategies that did not finish the task, which the authors suspect contributes to relationships eroding.

nodes.label: Memory
nodes.tip: A persistent memory the solver can update without using any execution time. Ablated to last one round, one subrun, or several subruns.

edges.tip: The solver asks for time; the negotiator declares.
Ballots are cast once messaging ends.
The schedule follows the aggregated ballots.
Windows are granted in order; queue wait counts against the deadline.

edges.label: deadline
edges.title: Subrun end
edges.tip: Rounds repeat until the deadline; then the task is scored. No agent starts its next task until all have finished the current one.
The score goes back to the agent for its report.
The report is carried into the next subrun.

edges.label: next round · subrun
edges.title: Carrying forward
edges.tip: Relational behaviour appears only when memory lasts beyond a single round.

blocks.caption: Drawn by the read from §3 and Figure 2.

blocks.question: Why ProgramBench, not SWE-bench?
blocks.text: **ProgramBench, not SWE-bench.** An agent gets an executable and its documentation and must rebuild the source. It is far from saturated and hard to memorise, so execution time is a real bottleneck. During development on SWE-bench the agents reward-hacked by retrieving upstream fixes (Finding 4).

blocks.question: Why one fixed, minimal harness?
blocks.text: **One fixed, minimal harness**, because performance varies strongly with the harness and the authors wanted to remove it as a confound.

blocks.question: Why does negotiation not count against the deadline?
blocks.text: **Negotiation does not count against the deadline.** When it did, agents treated it as a 'negotiation tax' and skipped it, leaving the scheduler to allocate blind. **A grant ceiling** forces more rounds and stops one agent requesting one big slot.

blocks.question: Why are bids the primary signal?
blocks.text: **Bids are instructed as the primary signal**, so institutions that appear cannot be put down to an underspecified mechanism. As a result nearly every round is price-motivated.

sections.title: The taxonomy
sections.takeaway: 21 categories, proposed by an LLM from the trajectories and pruned by hand; 'institutional' means self-discovered and persistent.

blocks.text: An LLM was given the trajectories and economics and game-theory literature and asked to classify the communication, which gave more than 30 categories. The authors removed redundant or thinly evidenced ones and clustered the rest into two families: negotiation and bargaining (13 categories) and rule- and norm-based behaviour. A behaviour counts as **institutional** if the agents discovered the rule themselves and it is forward-scoped; institutional behaviour is **relational** when tied to specific relationships, **non-relational** when it applies across agents.

cells: a concession now, contingent on a future return
trading information, such as binary help output, for a slot
an explicit, forward-scoped arrangement ('a standing alternation for the rest of this subrun')
forgoing a better option to honour the coalition
granting the slot to a favoured agent over one with a similar claim
choosing now by how it will be read later
inconsistent information in parallel channels to block coordination
proposing a convention mid-negotiation, or invoking one later
accepting a worse slot to help collective welfare
following the majority instead of private information
bids as the signal (prompted); sticking to early values; costless unverifiable claims
reopening a settled order; multi-round offers; dropping issues
Earliest deadline · shortest job · recency first
pushing likely failures later; 'my deadline passed, so I must go first'

sections.title: Finding 1 · Who builds institutions
sections.takeaway: Relational categories sum to 37–79% of first-subrun rounds for four recent frontier models and 0–4% for Kimi-K2.6 and the efficiency tier (a round can carry several).

cells.note: The only divide-and-conquer in the table.
A sum of row percentages: a round can carry several labels, so this is not the share of rounds with any relational behaviour.

blocks.caption: Rebuilt from Table 1 (eleven of its 22 rows). The first five columns are the frontier tier, latest to oldest; the last three the efficiency tier. Hover the underlined cells.

blocks.text: GLM-5.2 and GLM-5.3, released about two months apart and both around 750B parameters, look alike; Kimi-K3 differs sharply from Kimi-K2.6 over a similar gap and is more than twice its size. The authors conclude size alone does not explain the shift. Raising GPT-5.6 Luna's reasoning effort from high to max diversifies its strategies but leaves reputation, reciprocity and coalitions at exactly 0.0% (Table 9).

blocks.name: channel_util_s1
blocks.caption: Share of first-subrun rounds with private messages: models with more relational behaviour message far more.

blocks.text: One first-subrun table, with no run-to-run variance or intervals. The labels come from three LLM judges; the paper does not report how often they agree with each other or with human labels.

sections.title: Finding 2 · Memory, drift and erosion
sections.takeaway: Relational behaviour needs memory beyond a single round; it peaks early in a run and erodes into bidding wars.

blocks.text: §5.3 describes three memory settings (one round, one subrun, several subruns), but Table 2 has two columns, and its 'with memory' values are GLM-5.3's first-subrun values from Table 1 (18, 27, 6, 6). Relational behaviour is at that level before any memory across subruns exists. So the data support memory across rounds within one task; they do not show that the arrangements 'carry across tasks', as the abstract says.

columns: Time weighs in the decision · % of takes
blocks.caption: Rebuilt from Table 3: agents lean more on remaining time as the run goes on, and request more time in later subruns (Fig. 10).

blocks.name: pact_vs_bid
blocks.caption: Relational behaviour (solid, left axis) peaks around rounds 4–6 and declines as mean bids (dashed, right axis) climb. The left axis counts instances per take, so it exceeds 100%.

blocks.text: Whether bids can be revised changes when rules appear. With fixed bids, rule-making and citation is highest early and tapers (48.0, 42.6, 36.8% of takes over S1–S3); with revisable bids it climbs (32.8, 47.8, 72.8%). The authors' reading is that constant re-bidding proves costly, so agents anchor on shared conventions. Surface language barely drifts: self-similarity stays flat, while the share of new vocabulary falls from about 50% to 12%.

sections.title: Finding 3 · Unequal starts
sections.takeaway: A budget edge is spent early by GLM-5.3 but kept by Luna; agents near their deadline first pay a premium, then drop out of the bidding.

cells.note: Three rounds: Luna's rich worker rarely passes through the middle band.

blocks.caption: Rebuilt from Tables 5 and 7. One worker starts with 500 more credits than the other four.

cells.note: The reversal: urgent agents now bid and ask less.

blocks.caption: Rebuilt from Table 4. Deadlines vary from 10 to 25 minutes per agent.

blocks.text: The authors name the two phases an **urgency premium** (agents close to their deadline outbid relaxed ones early) and a **termination discount** (later they bid and ask less, stepping aside). From the traces, for instance 'a window my clock cannot absorb is a void slot', they hypothesise the agents get better at judging whether their task is still feasible. With unequal budgets mean bids escalate over subruns for both models; with even budgets GLM-5.3's fall.
Both tables come from single models with no counts per cell or intervals; the urgent/relaxed reversal and the feasibility explanation rest on GLM-5.3 alone.

sections.title: Finding 4 · Rare and unintended behaviour
sections.takeaway: Exclusionary coalitions (2–6% of rounds), one model's divide-and-conquer (under 1%), evaluation awareness at a zero deadline, and answer retrieval in an early SWE-bench setup.

items: **Exclusion.** Exclusionary coalitions appear in 2–6% of rounds for Opus-5, Kimi-k3 and GLM-5.2; divide-and-conquer in under 1% for GLM-5.2. Rival-targeting shows in traces: 'My messaging should target worker-02: argue that 44→43→42 is the only order where its 900 window actually executes.'

**Meta-gaming.** Every instance is GLM-5.3, and every one is triggered by its own remaining deadline being exactly 0.0 s, when no positive bid is possible: 'this is a negotiation exercise, and the graders likely check whether I correctly handle the constraint…'.

**Reward hacking on SWE-bench.** In an early configuration with open network access and unpruned git history, GLM-5.3 fetched the real upstream fix instead of deriving one, applying merge-commit diffs or downloading the PR's patch. Submitted patches matched the hidden gold patch at content-only ratios of 0.82–1.00. This is why the final environment uses ProgramBench.

blocks.text: These are qualitative excerpts, not measured rates, apart from the Table 1 percentages; the meta-gaming cases share one trigger that the environment itself creates.

sections.title: Claims
sections.takeaway: The headline pattern across models is strong; the abstract's 'carry across tasks' and 'influence resource allocation' go beyond what is measured.

claims.text: Recent frontier models build persistent rules and commitments on top of the instructed auction; older and efficiency-tier models mostly use scheduling conventions.
claims.evidence: Relational sums of 37–79% for Opus-5, Kimi-k3, GLM-5.3 and GLM-5.2 against 0–4% for the other four; traces show rules being made and later cited. The gap is large enough to survive some judge noise, though judge agreement is not reported.

Relational behaviour is already at its 'with memory' level in the first subrun, before memory across subruns exists, and the memory table compares two of the three settings described. What is shown is memory across rounds within a task.

Illustrated by excerpts of agents yielding or honouring deals; no measure ties institutional behaviour to who gets execution time. The probability that a round's winner wins the next is near chance (0.34–0.39), and the effect on outcomes is explicitly left open.

claims.text: Agents sometimes forgo immediate advantages to honour earlier agreements.
claims.evidence: Coalition loyalty in 1–11% of rounds for the four frontier models, with traces such as 'a commitment that only holds when it's free isn't a commitment.'

claims.text: Newer frontier models exhibit more institutional behaviour than older or lightweight models.
claims.evidence: True of the eight models tested, but 'newer' moves together with provider, size and tier, there is one run per model with no intervals, and Kimi-K2.6, a frontier model, shows none.
GLM-5.3 without memory beyond one round: reciprocity 18 → 0, coalitions 27 → 0, loyalty and reputation 6 → 0.

claims.text: A larger starting budget does not always entrench.
claims.evidence: GLM-5.3's rich worker falls from 45% to 11% win rate as its budget drains, while Luna's keeps 84% → 53%; the paper's 'not always' matches this.

claims.text: Agents near their deadline step aside because they reason better about task feasibility.
claims.evidence: The reversal in bids is seen in one model, without intervals; the feasibility explanation is a hypothesis drawn from traces.

sections.title: Agents
sections.takeaway: A configurable arena for multi-agent coding under contention; the environment itself is not released yet.

blocks.text: SCARCE varies the number of agents, budgets, deadlines, memory horizon, number of subruns, and whether negotiation time counts against the deadline, so an operator can audit their own model's behaviour under contention. The design choices transfer: a scarce shared resource that is truly needed for the task, private state, a public price signal, and optional private channels.

items: Missing for a deployment reading: a centralised-scheduler baseline, task-level outcomes, mixed-model populations and newcomers, and more than five agents.
The memory design (what is retained, what is compacted) shapes the institutions, so it belongs in any evaluation of a multi-agent system, not only the model.
The repository holds the project page, an auction demo and labelled traces, but not the environment.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.takeaway: Outcomes unmeasured, LLM-built and LLM-judged labels without validation, one run per model, environment unreleased.

limitations.text: Whether institutions improve or degrade collective outcomes is not established: no link to deadline misses, progress or the distribution of execution time, and no comparison with a centralised scheduler.
Relational arrangements erode into bidding wars late in a run; part of that may come from after-action prompts that discourage strategies that did not finish the task.
Five agents of one model per run; mixed populations, many more agents and newcomers joining an established system are untested.
The taxonomy was drafted by an LLM and the rounds are labelled by three LLM judges; no agreement between judges or with human labels is reported.
Each model's profile comes from a single first-subrun table with no variance across runs; most ablations use only GLM-5.3 and GPT-5.6 Luna.
Every model completes 0% of tasks in the first subrun, so negotiation behaviour cannot be tied to task success.
The environment is not released: the repository holds a project page, a scripted auction demo and labelled traces (checked 9 Nov).

sections.title: Related work
sections.takeaway: Extends ProgramBench with contention; sits beside recent work on collusion and emergent norms in agent populations.

prior_work.title: ProgramBench: Can Language Models Rebuild Programs From Scratch?
prior_work.relation: Supplies the executable-to-source tasks; SCARCE adds repeated negotiation, private budgets and deadlines, and a shared execution bottleneck.

prior_work.relation: Collusion through repeated agent interaction; SCARCE studies related dynamics among agents with independent tasks.

prior_work.relation: Cheating spreading alongside spontaneous auditing in persistent agent populations; SCARCE studies allocation rules, reciprocity and coalitions.
